passage:
Lights-out at the residential school hostel was at ten, but Naveen was still under his torch with a physics workbook. Baljeet leaned over from the top bunk.
'You're always saying whatever is written will happen. So why kill yourself over numericals?'
Naveen smiled without looking up. 'My Dadi says the pen is ours and the page is God's.' He underlined a formula. 'I do my part. The rest isn't mine to fret over.'
'And last year? When you missed the science olympiad by one mark?'
Naveen was quiet a moment. 'I cried that night. Then I thought, maybe it wasn't meant to be that year. It let me sleep. But I still went back and found the mark I lost.'
Baljeet flopped back onto the pillow. 'Weird. But it works for you.'

qa.q: By how many marks did Naveen miss the science olympiad?
qa.a: By one mark.

qa.q: What did Naveen feel the night he missed the olympiad, and what brought him peace?
qa.a: He was upset enough to cry, and the thought that it wasn't meant to be that year calmed him enough to sleep.

qa.q: What choice did Naveen make after that loss that kept the work in his own hands?
qa.a: He went back and found the mark he lost, so his belief in fate comforted him without stopping him from improving.

qa.q: How does Baljeet see Naveen's way of holding fate and effort together?
qa.a: Baljeet finds it odd, even contradictory, at first, but admits it seems to work for Naveen.

grounding: Shows a teenager from a traditional home who trusts destiny, finds peace after a loss through it, and still studies hard and owns his part.

passage:
Dear Ankita Didi,
The water has gone down now. We lost most of the stock in the shop: the rice sacks, the notebooks, even Baba's old ledger. Ma sat on the steps that first evening and said, 'What was written, was written.' I thought she would be broken, but she seemed almost peaceful, and somehow that made me calm too.
I believe that as well, Didi. Some things come from above. But the boards are in March, and nobody above is going to learn trigonometry for me. So I study at the neighbour's house in the mornings and help Baba sort the dry stock in the evenings.
The flood took the shop's goods. It didn't take my pencil.
Write soon,
Binita

qa.q: What did the family lose when the water came?
qa.a: Most of the stock in the shop: the rice sacks, the notebooks and even Baba's old ledger.

qa.q: Why did Binita feel calm after the flood?
qa.a: Seeing Ma almost peaceful, trusting that what was written was written, helped Binita feel calm as well.

qa.q: What choice did Binita make that kept both faith and effort alive?
qa.a: Binita chose to study at the neighbour's house in the mornings and help Baba in the evenings, accepting the loss without leaving the boards to fate.

qa.q: How might Ankita Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She might feel relieved that Binita is coping calmly and proud of the steady studying, while also sad about the family's losses.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose family's belief in fate brings peace after a loss, while the teenager keeps taking responsibility for studying.

passage:
"You're still studying, Eshaan? It's past eleven."
"Boards in two weeks, Ma."
Sonali sat on the edge of his bed. "Your Dadaji used to say, 'Do your karma, leave the fruit to God.'"
"I know. I think about that a lot since he died." Eshaan closed his book. "It helps, actually. Thinking it was his time. Not something anyone could stop."
"And the studying?"
"That's the karma part. God isn't going to learn trigonometry for me."
Sonali laughed. "Your Dadaji would have liked that line."
"I miss him."
"So do I, beta. Now sleep. The fruit will come when it comes."

qa.q: How long is it until Eshaan's boards?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: How does Eshaan feel when he thinks of it as his Dadaji's time?
qa.a: It gives him some peace in his grief, though he still misses his Dadaji.

qa.q: How does Eshaan hold fate and effort together?
qa.a: He accepts his grandfather's death as fate while seeing studying as his own duty, the karma part.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel hearing Eshaan's trigonometry line?
qa.a: Sonali feels warm and amused, glad to hear her father-in-law's saying live on in her son.

grounding: Shows a teen from a traditional home finding peace after a loss in fate while still taking responsibility through study.

passage: When the list for the state science camp came out and my name wasn't on it, my Ammi said, "Naseeb mein nahi tha." It wasn't written. I'm Zeenat, fifteen, and for a day I was angry at that, as if it meant my work didn't count. Then my cousin Salma said, "It means you can stop punishing yourself for it. Not that you stop." That helped. I did work hard. Someone else also worked hard, and there were only four places. I prayed that evening and felt, strangely, lighter. Next morning I was at the kitchen table at six with my physics book, because next year's list isn't written yet. Allah decides; I still show up.

qa.q: How many places were there at the camp?
qa.a: Four places.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel after praying that evening?
qa.a: Zeenat felt strangely lighter and more at peace, after a day of anger.

qa.q: What did Salma's words help Zeenat understand?
qa.a: That fate can ease self-blame without meaning Zeenat should stop working.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Zeenat studying at six the next morning?
qa.a: Ammi would likely feel proud, seeing faith and hard work sitting together.

grounding: Shows a teen who holds belief in destiny together with hard work, finding peace after a setback without giving up responsibility.

passage: Class teacher's note, Monday. Kavitha returned after ten days away; her grandmother died during the Pongal holidays. I expected her to be behind or withdrawn. She was quiet, but she handed in every assignment. When I asked how she was, she said, "Paati's time had come. Amma says what's written is written. That gives me some peace." Then she asked for the notes she'd missed and whether she could stay after school for the chemistry practical. Her younger brother Dhruv, in Class 6, is struggling more; he cried in assembly. I have let the counsellor know about both, and I will check in with Kavitha each Friday.

qa.q: How long was Kavitha away?
qa.a: Ten days.

qa.q: What helps Kavitha feel some peace about her grandmother's death?
qa.a: The belief that Paati's time had come, which eases her grief.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that was wise?
qa.a: Noticed how each child was coping, told the counsellor about both and planned weekly check-ins with Kavitha.

qa.q: How might Dhruv be experiencing the loss differently?
qa.a: Dhruv seems more openly upset, crying in assembly, and may need more support than his sister.

grounding: Shows a teen whose belief in fate brings peace after a loss while she keeps up her studies and responsibilities.

passage:
14 August, night
Dadi's first death anniversary today. We did the puja in the morning. Mummy said, "It was written, her time had come." Strangely, that helps me. I don't lie awake asking "what if we'd taken her to the hospital sooner" like I did last year. It feels like a calm place to put the sadness.
But then Jatin said, "If everything's written, why are you studying till eleven for the maths Olympiad?"
I laughed. Dadi used to say it too: "Bhagwan decides the harvest, but you still plough the field." I think both are true for me. Some things are not in my hands, like Dadi's illness. Some things are, like practising geometry.
So, I'll pray tonight. And then I'll do two more practice papers.
Jaya

qa.q: What was Jaya studying for?
qa.a: The maths Olympiad.

qa.q: How does the belief that "it was written" make Jaya feel about Dadi's death?
qa.a: It gives Jaya a calm, peaceful place to put the sadness, instead of lying awake with guilty "what if" questions.

qa.q: How does Jaya hold fate and effort together?
qa.a: Jaya accepts that some things, like Dadi's illness, are not in human hands, while still taking responsibility for what is, like practising geometry.

qa.q: Why might Jatin find Jaya's view puzzling?
qa.a: Jatin seems to think believing in fate should mean not trying, so studying till eleven looks like a contradiction to Jatin.

grounding: Shows a teen from a traditional home finding peace in fate after a grandmother's death while still studying hard, holding both together.
